summary: This document introduces a hub and spoke multipoint (HSMP) Label Switched Path, which carries traffic from the root to the leaves along a point-to-multipoint LSP and also from leaves back to the root along the reverse path. It does this with extensions to LDP.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7140 adds a hub and spoke label switched path to the Label Distribution Protocol, the protocol that MPLS routers use to set up paths. The path has one root node and one or more leaf nodes. Traffic sent from the root reaches every leaf, and traffic sent from a leaf reaches only the root. Leaves cannot send to each other directly.

subtitle: One root node reaches every leaf node over a label switched path, and each leaf reaches only the root.

tldr.problem: A point-to-multipoint path carries traffic only from one root to the leaves, and a multipoint-to-multipoint path lets every node reach every other node. Neither fits a design where the leaves must reach only the root.
tldr.mechanism: The hub and spoke multipoint path pairs a downstream point-to-multipoint tree with an upstream path that follows the same tree in reverse and ends only at the root. LDP gains two new FEC types (9 and 10), a capability parameter (0x0902) and label messages for both directions.
tldr.outcome: Leaves can send to the root and the root can send to all leaves, with no leaf-to-leaf traffic. RFC 7140 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 7358.

today: RFC 7140 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 7358. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The point-to-multipoint (P2MP) label switched path defined in RFC 6388 carries traffic from one ingress router to several egress routers. The multipoint-to-multipoint (MP2MP) path carries traffic from any node to every other node in the group. RFC 7140 adds a third shape: the hub and spoke multipoint (HSMP) path, with one root node and one or more leaf nodes.

An HSMP path has a downstream part and an upstream part. Traffic entering at the root travels downstream along the tree and arrives at every leaf, exactly as on a P2MP path. Traffic entering at any leaf travels upstream and reaches only the root. The upstream part follows the same tree in the reverse direction rather than the path that the routing protocol would pick, so the upstream direction is a multipoint-to-point path built from the upstream paths of all leaves.

Direct communication between leaf nodes is not allowed. A packet that a leaf sends reaches the root first, and the root then places it on the point-to-multipoint tree, which delivers it to every leaf, including the sender.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC adds a third kind of label switched path, called a hub and spoke path. It has one hub (the root) and one or more spokes (the leaves). Traffic from the hub reaches every spoke. Traffic from a spoke reaches only the hub, and spokes cannot send to each other.

sections.title: Terms and Acronyms
sections.content:
The RFC defines four path types. mLDP is the set of Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) extensions for multipoint paths, defined in RFC 6388. A P2MP LSP is a path with one ingress label switching router (LSR) and one or more egress LSRs. An MP2MP LSP connects a set of nodes so that traffic sent by any node in the path reaches all the others. An HSMP LSP has one root node and one or more leaf nodes, and carries traffic from the root to all leaves along the downstream P2MP path and from any leaf to the root along the upstream path.

The list also names FEC, the forwarding equivalence class. The RFC uses FEC elements to identify a path, and adds two new ones for this design.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC names four path types and one abbreviation. A P2MP path has one sender and several receivers. An MP2MP path lets every node reach every other node. An HSMP path has one root and one or more leaves, where the root reaches all leaves and each leaf reaches only the root. FEC is short for forwarding equivalence class.

sections.title: Setting Up an HSMP Path with LDP
sections.content:
An HSMP path is built like an MP2MP path, with one difference: when a leaf sends traffic, the traffic is delivered only to the root first, and the root then distributes it on the point-to-multipoint tree to all leaves.

The upstream part of the path MUST be set up in ordered mode. Ordered mode guarantees that a leaf can start sending packets to the root as soon as the upstream path is installed, instead of dropping packets because the path is not complete yet.

Nodes announce support with the HSMP LSP Capability Parameter, a new capability parameter TLV of type 0x0902. It is carried in Initialization and Capability messages, following the procedures for capability parameters in RFC 5561. The U-bit must be 1 and the F-bit must be 0, and the length should be 1.

Label messages that use an HSMP FEC element should not be sent to a peer that has not advertised the capability. The peer would break the label message, and the leaf that started it could not establish the upstream path to the root.
sections.plainLanguage: The upstream half of the path must be installed in ordered mode, so a leaf can send as soon as the path is ready instead of losing packets first. Each router advertises a capability message with code 0x0902 to say that it supports these paths. A router must not send HSMP label messages to a peer that has not advertised that capability.

sections.title: The HSMP FEC Elements and Label Messages
sections.content:
The RFC defines two new FEC element types: HSMP-upstream FEC (9) and HSMP-downstream FEC (10). A FEC TLV that contains one of these elements must contain nothing else. The structure, encoding and error handling are the same as for the P2MP FEC element described in RFC 6388.

Each HSMP FEC element holds the root node address X and an opaque value Y. On that pair the RFC defines the label messages used for the path: a downstream and an upstream label mapping, a downstream and an upstream label withdraw, and a downstream and an upstream label release. In a label mapping, the label is allocated by the router that sends the message, from its own platform label space.
sections.plainLanguage: Two new identifiers are defined for these paths: type 9 for the upstream half and type 10 for the downstream half. Each identifier carries the root address and a value chosen by the operator. The RFC then defines label mapping, label withdrawal and label release messages for each direction.

sections.title: Mapping, Withdrawing and Releasing Labels
sections.content:
A leaf node Z finds the upstream LSR U for the path, allocates a label L, and sends a downstream label mapping to U. When U answers with an upstream label mapping carrying a label Lu, Z installs forwarding state that pushes Lu onto the traffic it wants to send on this path. Which traffic belongs on the path is outside the scope of the RFC.

A transit node Z that receives a downstream label mapping from D allocates its own label L' and passes the mapping upstream, unless D is already the upstream LSR for the path. For the upstream direction, Z waits until the upstream LSR U has assigned a label Lu, then allocates its own label Lu' and sends an upstream label mapping back down toward D. Because a packet from any downstream node goes only to the upstream node, the same upstream label can be distributed to all downstream nodes. This differs from MP2MP, where each downstream node needs a distinct label.

The root behaves differently. It never sends a downstream label mapping and never receives an upstream label mapping. When it receives an upstream label mapping, it creates forwarding state for the incoming label that pops the label stack and passes the packet to an application, which makes the root the egress label edge router for the path. The root may also be a leaf node.

Withdrawal follows the tree backwards. A leaf that no longer needs to be an egress router sends a downstream label withdraw to its upstream LSR and an unsolicited upstream label release, and expects a downstream label release in reply. A transit node that receives the withdraw deletes the label and releases it downstream. If nothing is left, it propagates the withdraw upstream and releases the upstream state. The root does the same but does not propagate further, because it has no upstream.
sections.plainLanguage: Each leaf picks the router that leads to the root, hands it a label, and waits for that router to send a label back. When the reply arrives, the leaf can forward traffic onto the path. Transit routers do the same in both directions and pass one shared upstream label to every node below them. The root ends the path by popping the label and giving the packet to the application.

sections.title: Running an HSMP Path over a LAN
sections.content:
On a LAN, the downstream part of an HSMP path is handled like a downstream MP2MP path. When the downstream path is established, a Label Request message for an LSP label is sent to the upstream LSR. The upstream LSR answers with a Label Mapping message that holds the LSP label for the downstream HSMP FEC and the upstream LSR context label defined in RFC 5331.

When the upstream LSR forwards a packet downstream, the top label must be the upstream LSR context label and the second label must be the LSP label. The downstream path is installed in the context-specific forwarding table that belongs to the upstream LSR label, so the upstream LSR can forward downstream packets with a two-label lookup.

The upstream part of the path works the same way on a LAN as on other links: the upstream LSR sends a Label Mapping message with the LSP label for the upstream HSMP FEC, and packets travelling upstream are forwarded towards the root with that label.
sections.plainLanguage: On a shared LAN segment the downstream part of the path uses two labels. The top label identifies the segment, and the second label identifies the path. Packets sent upstream use a single label, the one allocated for the upstream part of the path.

sections.title: Redundancy and Failure Detection
sections.content:
For redundancy, an operator can run two independent HSMP paths, one active and one standby. Only one is active at a time. After the active path fails is detected, the root and the leaf nodes move the traffic to the standby path, which then acts as the active one. The RFC leaves the details of the redundancy mechanism out of scope.

Failure detection can use the LSP ping mechanism. The root sends an LSP Ping Echo Request that enters along a downstream path of the HSMP path and ends its MPLS path on the leaf. The leaf sends the LSP Ping Echo Reply along the upstream path, and it ends on the root.

To make sure the reply follows the upstream path, the R flag, the Validate Reverse Path flag in the Global Flags field defined in RFC 6426, is reused. The root must attach the Target FEC Stack TLV with the HSMP-downstream FEC type and set the R flag to 1. The leaf must send the reply along the associated HSMP upstream path, and the Reverse-path Target FEC Stack TLV in the reply should carry the sub-TLV of the associated HSMP-upstream FEC. The rest of the node processing is inherited from RFC 6425 and Section 3.4 of RFC 6426.
sections.plainLanguage: An operator can run a second copy of the path and keep it on standby. If the first one fails, traffic moves to the standby. To notice a failure, the root sends a test packet down the path; the leaf answers along the upstream path, which proves both halves still work.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that the same security considerations apply as for the MP2MP path described in RFC 6388 and RFC 6425. Although it introduces new FEC elements and new procedures, the protocol brings no new security issues beyond those already set out in those two documents.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC adds no security problems of its own. It says that the same protections apply as for the multipoint-to-multipoint path and for LSP ping.
